title: Why does a random UUIDv4 primary key hurt write performance (B-tree page splits, index bloat, worse on InnoDB), and how do you fix it with UUIDv7, ULID, or a sequential id?
shortTitle: Why does random UUID primary key hurt performance?
keyPoints: A random UUIDv4 has no ordering, so each insert lands at a random position in the B-tree causing page splits and fragmentation.
Page splits are expensive: a full leaf page must split and move half its rows, leaving both pages half-full.
Poor cache locality: each insert touches a different page, thrashing the buffer pool once the table outgrows memory.
InnoDB is worst because the primary key IS the clustered index that physically orders the row data, and every secondary index stores the full PK.
The fix is a time-ordered identifier: UUIDv7, ULID, or sequential bigint so inserts append near the end of the B-tree.
Keep a sequential or time-ordered clustered PK internally and expose a separate random UUID as the external public identifier.

s1_definition.oneliner: Random UUIDv4 as a PK scatters inserts across the B-tree causing page splits, fragmentation, and cache misses; fix with time-ordered UUIDv7, ULID, or sequential bigint so inserts append.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **B-tree page split** – when a new key must be inserted into a full leaf page, the page splits in half, creating two half-full pages and extra I/O.
- **Index fragmentation** – after many splits, pages are half-full and scattered, wasting disk and memory.
- **Cache/buffer-pool thrash** – with random keys, each insert touches a different page, so the working set does not fit in memory and inserts hit disk.
- **Clustered index (InnoDB)** – the primary key physically orders the row data, so a random PK scatters the actual rows, not just an index.
- **Time-ordered id (UUIDv7/ULID)** – encodes a timestamp in the high bits so values sort in insertion order, making inserts append-friendly.
- **Dual-id pattern** – use a sequential clustered PK internally for storage efficiency and expose a separate random UUID as the external public identifier.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India files transactions in a giant sorted ledger. A sequential id is like filing each new transaction at the BACK of the book: quick, the last page is always open on the desk. A random UUIDv4 is like inserting each transaction at a RANDOM page in the middle: the clerk constantly shoves existing entries aside to make room (page split), the book becomes full of half-empty pages (fragmentation), and the clerk must keep fetching different pages from the archive instead of keeping one open (cache misses).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Sequential Keys vs Random UUIDv4
  ============================================

  Sequential (BIGINT / UUIDv7):
  +------+------+------+------+
  | pg 1 | pg 2 | pg 3 | pg 4 | <- NEW rows append here
  | FULL | FULL | FULL | 70%  |
  +------+------+------+------+
  One hot page at the end. No splits. Cache hit.

  Random UUIDv4:
  +------+------+------+------+
  | pg 1 | pg 2 | pg 3 | pg 4 |
  | 50%  | 50%  | 50%  | 50%  | <- SPLIT everywhere
  +------+------+------+------+
  Every insert targets a random page.
  Page full -> SPLIT -> two half-full pages.
  Different page every time -> cache MISS.

  InnoDB Clustered Index Impact:
  ============================================
  Primary key = physical row order.
  Random PK = random row order in data file.

  Secondary indexes store [column, PK]:
  +-------------------------+
  | BIGINT PK:  8 bytes     | <- small secondary index
  | UUID PK:    16 bytes    | <- 2x larger secondary index
  +-------------------------+
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A random UUIDv4 has no ordering, so when used as a primary-key index every insert lands at a random position in the B-tree rather than appending at the end. That causes page splits, index fragmentation, and cache thrash. It is worst on MySQL InnoDB because the primary key physically orders the row data itself, so a random PK scatters the actual rows, and every secondary index stores the full primary key, making them all larger.

The fix is a time-ordered identifier so inserts append near the end of the index while staying globally unique. At National Bank of India, Rajesh switched the transactions table from random UUIDv4 to UUIDv7 using Hibernate's @UuidGenerator(style=TIME), which kept the globally-unique, app-generatable id for the distributed ledger nodes but made inserts append again.

The senior nuance Pankaj adds is that if the team needs a random, non-guessable identifier for external exposure, they keep a sequential bigint or UUIDv7 as the internal clustered primary key and expose a separate random UUID as the public id with its own index. That way they get fast append-friendly inserts internally and non-sequential, non-guessable ids externally.

Remember one sentence: random UUIDv4 as a clustered primary key causes page splits and index fragmentation; use time-ordered UUIDv7, ULID, or sequential bigint so inserts append.
